why: Simpler three-question frame, concrete, ends with an action for the student's own bet; A is a dated citation list.
Personal story gives the closing line its meaning; B drops the setup so 'the blur' has no referent.
Asks for the guess before the reveal, which makes the prediction exercise work; B reveals first and then asks.
Says what happens next, shaping the rules together, instead of a bare negation.
Tells the student what to do with a mismatch, which completes the spot-check.
'Session' is the controlled term; 'run' is a loose synonym.
The title states the claim, and B's generic 'The generalisation' title is weaker. B's added line is a good closer, but the title carries more.
Ties back to the M6 encode loop and closes with the flywheel line.
Leaner; B's added 'shape the whole map has had from the start' is a vague claim.
Ends on the concrete instruction; B's extra line is a vague moral.
'M6 exercise' is the right term for what was run; 'prompts' is less accurate.
Same meaning; 'this session's scrollback' is clearer than 'this scrollback'.
B forward-references Module 4 and is vague; A ends on a clear, usable practitioner default.
Opening is more direct and compact; A's 'runs on' phrasing is clunkier.

B's forward reference to Phases 3 and 4 adds clutter; A ends cleanly on the point.

A avoids a count that is wrong, since the slide names verification, absorption and outcome but the lead-in is looser; 'new concerns' is safe.
'Three pressures' matches the three bullets and is more concrete.
'Three agents using the file' is a concrete, picturable header that matches the three bullets.

B is punchier, with more concrete story beats (re-sim, ten fixes, pushback on 'done'), and a shorter list of numbers.

B's opening bullet is a fragment that pre-empts the point made in the following lines; A goes straight to the claim.
'Check what Claude proposes' is more active and plainer than 'Read', which fits the student judging the agent's work.
The forest-before-trees image is picturable and memorable, and A's point is flatter.
'A check resets the chain' is a concrete, picturable claim; B's title is wordier.
A's title is an instruction that states the action; B's is a general statement that is less useful.

A names the ADR plainly; B's 'hardening call a future engineer can inspect' is vaguer and puts the acronym in parentheses.
A names 'the wall' as a bolded, reusable concept that the slide then uses as its recurring metaphor.
A's title makes a concrete, picturable claim, and the body's Slack-thread contrast supports it directly.
Shorter title; 'window' already clear from the body, so nothing is lost.
The closing line states the point plainly and gives the slide a memorable takeaway.
'Five things' sets a count the room can track, and the list does have five items.
It tells the student what to ask Claude, so the exercise is clearer than the bare 'Spot what's still generic' line.

Dropping 'You don't need to get it right first time' keeps the slide to claims and instructions, without reassuring the student.
It is concrete and actionable. B is abstract and its 'consume' and 'walks the branches you may not see' are muddy.
It is cleaner, and B's added connective lines are filler between the links.
'Alternatives' is plainer than 'committed change', which is confusing next to git commits, and it reads clearly in the room.
